title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1, preregistration SHA-256 archived) to measure whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes using 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). A preregistered planning assumption (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, artifact‑grounded confirmatory statistics, an explicit explanation of the McNemar outcome given the observed discordant count, and practical recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. Key artifacts cited in the paper are archived and hashed in the execution manifest.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is foundational to NetOps automation. Large language models (LLMs) promise rapid intent→configuration synthesis but are probabilistic and can produce unsafe misordering or omissions. A common mitigation pattern pairs a probabilistic generator with deterministic validators/simulators and bounded repair loops (generate→verify→repair). However, there is limited preregistered, artifact‑archived evidence that quantifies how narrowly bounded guarded pipelines affect first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics. We ask: Can a minimal guarded pipeline—one shared single‑shot LLM candidate per task, a frozen deterministic validator, and at most one automated repair iteration—reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a paired design? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic task seeds and full archival of per‑task artifacts; (2) confirmatory statistics directly computed from archived artifacts; (3) an explicit artifact‑grounded explanation of the observed inferential outcome; and (4) concrete, artifact‑traceable recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory studies.
sections.related_work: Recent work demonstrates promising LLM‑based intent→configuration synthesis in testbeds but consistently reports operational failure modes (misordering, omission, overconfidence) that threaten safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Studies in adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) show that verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented pipelines reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating guarded NetOps architectures [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Deterministic network verification techniques (e.g., header‑space/ specification checking) provide algorithmic mechanisms to statically assert reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Surveys and evaluation‑architecture proposals emphasize generate→verify→repair patterns and the need for reproducible artifact capture, auditability, and careful experimental design [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our experiment situates itself at the intersection of these strands by executing a preregistered paired test with deterministic seeds and validator traces to quantify a narrowly defined operational effect.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered the study as cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA-256 recorded) before observing outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration included a planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40 used for power calculations; that assumption is reported here because it materially affects confirmatory interpretation.

Design and sampling semantics: Paired within‑task design with a frozen deterministic seed list of 300 tasks; each seed produced an intent and a canonical reference configuration. For operational realism we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single LLM candidate per seed served as both the baseline response and the starting point for guarded validation/repair. Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1.

Model and sampling configuration: The declared model in the execution contract/artifact was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA-256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). That artifact records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null. Because temperature was unset (null) in the archived model configuration, the run does not establish an explicit fixed sampling temperature; sampling determinism is therefore unspecified (provider default) and is a caveat for generalization. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics partially mitigate sampling variability by using the same generated candidate for both arms, but unspecified provider sampling remains a factor.

Validator and repair: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized outputs to a normalized AST and applied static checks derived from task payload workflow policies; scoring required full intent‑constraint validation (normalized configuration satisfies the task's required_sequence and expected_final_state and no workflow violations). The repair adapter was invoked only when the validator reported violations, received structured violation codes plus the shared candidate, and was limited to one automated repair attempt per episode; repair responses were revalidated by the same deterministic validator.

Primary estimand and analysis: Primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test = exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired binary outcomes; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) for the absolute paired difference were preregistered. Repair effectiveness (H2) is assessed conditional on initial failure; Clopper–Pearson CIs are reported for repair counts. All design rules, exclusion/replacement policies, and missingness treatments were preregistered and are archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair invocation). No provider/infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy.

Primary outcomes (archived counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). The paired contingency derived from archived analysis artifact analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA-256: 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55) is: n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00 for these counts. Absolute paired difference = (n10 − n01)/N = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap seed = 1729).

Why p = 1.00: The exact McNemar test conditions on the total number of discordant pairs (n10 + n01 = 1). With only one discordant pair, the conditional null distribution is degenerate for two‑sided testing and cannot produce a small p‑value for moderate effect sizes; hence the test returns p = 1.00 for the observed ordering (n10=1, n01=0). The archived paired contingency and bootstrap parameters are the authoritative source for this arithmetic and the reported CI.

Repair outcomes (H2): The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1). Clopper–Pearson 95% CI for 1/1 = [0.025, 1.0], reflecting extreme imprecision from a single observed repair.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation: The observed near‑ceiling baseline (299/300) contradicts the preregistered planning assumption (baseline = 0.40) and eliminated the discordant pairs needed to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. For N=300, absolute paired difference equals (n10 − n01)/300, so an absolute +0.30 would require ~90 net discordant pairs favoring guarded outputs—far larger than the single discordant pair observed. These arithmetic facts follow directly from archived counts.

Design implications: (1) When planning confirmatory generate→verify→repair experiments, explicitly link pairing semantics (shared candidate vs independent draws) to the estimand and incorporate their effect on expected discordant counts into power/sample‑size calculations. Shared_candidate pairing models remediation of a single plan (higher ecological validity) but reduces expected discordance and therefore inferential power for a given marginal success rate. (2) If repair effectiveness is a primary claim, ensure the study is powered for the conditional estimand P(repair succeeds | initial failure) by calibrating task difficulty or adversarially increasing initial failure prevalence. (3) To claim runtime semantic safety, integrate emulation/simulation stages; static deterministic validation suffices for many policy checks but cannot capture control‑plane convergence or transient dataplane effects.

Validator traces and reproducibility: Deterministic validator traces (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied) are essential for failure‑mode analysis and reproducible auditing. The execution manifest records per‑task artifacts and model call accounting and is the authoritative archive for the reported counts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (declared: gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline (frozen deterministic validator + one automated repair). Observed results: baseline 299/300 valid, guarded 300/300 valid; paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; exact McNemar p = 1.00; absolute paired difference ≈ 0.00333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01]. The single allowed repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output (1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption baseline = 0.40 was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction claim and rendering H1 infeasible to test as a confirmatory large‑effect hypothesis in this run. Practical recommendations (artifact‑traceable): preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly; calibrate task difficulty or adversarially seed failures to attain planned discordant counts; include emulation when runtime semantics are required. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single declared LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Shared_initial_candidate pairing increased within‑pair correlation and therefore reduced the number of informative discordant pairs available to McNemar inference for a given marginal success rate.

Validation used deterministic static configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects (control‑plane convergence, transient dataplane behavior); runtime consequences were not executed and remain unmeasured.

Repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
